The Great Wall—one of the Seven Wonders of the World! Truly an unforgettable experience. We recommend starting early (around 7:30 AM) to beat the crowds. By the time we finished around 11:30, it was packed and hard to get clear photos—so the earlier, the better! We had hoped to catch the sunrise, but the site only opens at 7:30, so that’s good to know in advance. Tickets can be purchased at the entrance, and there’s a small market area with basic coffee (don’t expect too much!) and plenty of vendors along the way—feel free to browse and negotiate prices. Traveling with three kids and three tired broken legs(ours), we took it easy—rode the cable car up and the toboggan down, which the kids absolutely loved! In between, we walked, laughed, ate and took lots of photos, soaking in every moment of this incredible place. Tip: bring water, good shoes, and patience—it’s a climb worth every step. A once-in-a-lifetime family experience—absolutely must-do! 🏯✨ It’s my second - highly suggest to climb a different part every time. 🤨

The Great Wall of China is one of the most iconic and remarkable monuments in the world. Stretching thousands of kilometers across mountains, deserts, and valleys, it stands as a powerful symbol of China’s rich history, strength, and architectural excellence. Built over several centuries by different dynasties, the wall was mainly constructed for defense, but today it represents human determination and creativity. Visiting the Great Wall is a truly unforgettable experience. The structure is massive and well-preserved in many sections, allowing visitors to clearly see the advanced engineering techniques used in ancient times. Walking along the wall gives a strong sense of history, as each stone seems to tell a story of soldiers, builders, and emperors who contributed to its construction. The watchtowers and pathways add to the historical value and visual beauty of the site. The surrounding natural scenery greatly enhances the experience. From the top of the wall, visitors can enjoy breathtaking views of green hills, rugged mountains, and wide landscapes, making it a perfect place for photography and sightseeing. Popular sections such as Badaling and Mutianyu are well-managed, with proper facilities, clear signs, and safety measures for tourists. Overall, the Great Wall of China is not just a historical landmark but a global heritage site that inspires respect and admiration. It is a must-visit destination for anyone interested in history, culture, and world-famous architecture. The Great Wall truly deserves its place among the greatest wonders of the world.

I can confidently say that visiting the Mutianyu section of the Great Wall was the absolute highlight of my trip to China. I chose Mutianyu specifically because it’s known for being less crowded than Badaling, and it completely delivered. You need to see this. I visited on Mid September, 2025, and the weather was glorious—clear, blue skies and comfortably cool, which is ideal. I opted for the enclosed 10 min cable car ride, and it was worth every penny. The journey up offers stunning, panoramic views of the Wall snaking endlessly across the mountain ridges. The cable car delivers you right up to Watchtower 14, saving your energy for exploring the Wall itself. It’s perfect for maximizing your time and enjoying the scenery without having to climb the steep!!!!! access steps. The Wall views are simply breathtaking. Mutianyu is beautifully restored, allowing you to appreciate the sheer engineering prowess of the Ming Dynasty. The watchtowers are densely packed, and you can see unique features like the double-sided battlements (allowing defenders to fire in both directions). I do recommend to go Early even in mid-September, getting there early helps you beat any lingering crowds. And walk at least a few towers in both directions from Watchtower 14 to appreciate the different inclines and viewpoints. This has been an unforgettable experience. Mutianyu offers the perfect balance of historical grandeur, natural beauty, and modern convenience.

Mutianyu Great Wall has way fewer crowds than Badaling—most Chinese folks head to Badaling, especially during national holidays, which you absolutely should avoid unless you want to be shoved along like you're floating in mid-air. Book in advance here. Heads up: besides the entrance ticket, you'll need a shuttle bus ticket too (you can opt for the free walk, but it's super far and all uphill—save your energy for the Wall). Once off the shuttle, you can take the cable car or hike up. Another key note: the cable cars are run by two different companies, so tickets aren't interchangeable. If you wanna minimize walking, my rec is to take the enclosed cable car up—it drops you at Tower 16. From there, stroll toward Tower 6, and it's mostly downhill the whole way—not as grueling. Then snag a ticket for the other company's toboggan slide (I think it's called SPEED). It's a bit pricier (though the round-trip is cheaper), but: 1) less walking, 2) no backtracking, and 3) that slide is seriously fun. Oh, and by the way, there are tons of cats hanging around the Great Wall entrance and even up on the Wall itself—you can pet them to your heart's content.

The Great Wall of China is one of the most iconic and awe-inspiring structures ever built by humankind. It's more than just a wall; it's a symbol of China's ancient strength, perseverance, and profound history. Here is a comprehensive overview of this world wonder. What is it? The Great Wall is not a single, continuous line but a series of fortifications made of stone, brick, tamped earth, wood, and other materials. It's a massive defensive system that includes: · Walls: The main barriers. · Watchtowers: For surveillance, signaling, and garrisoning troops. · Beacon Towers: Used for sending smoke (by day) and fire (by night) signals to communicate over long distances. · Fortresses and Passes: Strategic strongholds at key points, like mountains and trade routes. Key Facts & Figures · Length: This is a famous topic of debate. The total length of all its branches built across various dynasties is estimated at over 21,196 kilometers (13,171 miles). This measurement comes from a comprehensive national survey. · Age: Its construction spanned over 2,300 years, from the 7th century BC to the 17th century AD. · UNESCO Status: Designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. · Famous Saying: A famous Chinese saying goes, "你不到长城非好汉" — "He who has not climbed the Great Wall is not a true man." --- Why Was it Built? The primary purpose was defense and control. 1. Military Defense: To protect the Chinese states and empires from invasions and raids by nomadic groups from the north, most notably the Mongols and the Xiongnu. 2. Border Control: It regulated trade along the Silk Road, allowing the imposition of tariffs and control over the movement of people and goods. 3. Symbol of Power: It was a massive display of the emperor's power and ability to mobilize vast resources, serving as a psychological barrier as much as a physical one. --- A History Across Dynasties The Wall was built, rebuilt, and maintained by multiple dynasties. The most significant contributions came from: · Qin Dynasty (221–206 BC): The First Emperor of Qin, Qin Shi Huang, is most famous for linking and extending earlier walls built by various warring states. This created the first "Great" Wall. · Han Dynasty (206 BC – 220 AD): The Wall was extended far to the west into the Gobi Desert to protect the lucrative Silk Road trade routes. · Ming Dynasty (1368–1644): This was the golden age of the Great Wall. After defeating the Mongols, the Ming emperors constructed the most robust and elaborate sections we see today. They used bricks and stone to create formidable fortifications, complete with the iconic watchtowers. --- Famous Sections to Visit Not all parts of the Wall are the same. Here are the most popular sections for tourists: Section Characteristics Best For Badaling The most famous and restored. Close to Beijing. First-time visitors, elderly, those wanting an easy, accessible experience. (Can be very crowded) Mutianyu Also well-restored, but with more dramatic scenery and fewer crowds. Most visitors; a great balance of beauty and accessibility. Features a toboggan slide down! Jinshanling A "wild" but partially restored section with stunning, rugged views. Hikers and photographers. Offers a more authentic and challenging experience. Simatai Steep, rugged, and preserved in its original state. Adventurous hikers.

The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the historical northern borders of Imperial China as protection against various nomadic groups of enemies. The first walls date back to the 7th century BC. The successive dynasties expanded the wall system and later the Qin dynasty joined together its various sections. Mutianyu Great Wall, connected to Juyong Pass in the west and Gubeikou in the east, was initially built under the command of General Xu Da during the early Ming Dynasty on the ruins of the Northern Qi Dynasty Great Wall. This section connects Gugbeikou in the east and Juyongguan in the west, and has been a vital military defence for protecting the capital region since ancient times. It is well-preserved section and showcases the ancient charm of the Great Wall. After you arrive at this place, you walk for some time and catch the shuttle bus service. After getting down from the shuttle, you again climb up to a point from where you take the cable car. As soon as you leave the cable car, you finally start your climb on the wall. The walk and the climb is quite strenuous for Senior Citizens, like me, so the best way is to walk slowly. Unfortunately, there are not many places where you can stop and sit for a while but once you reach the top of the walk, you are struck by the sheer beauty of the wall around you. The total length of the wall is 21196.18 km and from east to the west there are 15 passes. It the took over 2000 years to build the total wall. Truly there is no place of earth as beautiful as this and it is a definitely must do. The wall is so well preserved and the Chinese government maintains it beautifully.

Notice**This is not about The Great Wall of China. This place is beautiful and worth to visit once in your life time. But this about the shop in the photo. My first time visiting the Great Wall in January—freezing cold, insanely early tour, and clearly not my smartest moment. No breakfast, no planning, just me and poor decision-making. The moment I arrived, all I could think about was getting something warm in my stomach. Instead of looking around (which I definitely should have), I walked straight into the first shop I saw because the staff were loudly selling hot coffee. Big mistake. I ordered without asking the price and ended up with a so-called “fresh coffee”, a small cup, that tasted exactly like instant coffee… for 35 yuan. Yes. That much. At that point, the coffee was already made, and politeness won over common sense. Only after walking toward the entrance did I notice—there were plenty of other cafés around. That’s when it hit me: I had totally been ripped off. Lesson learned: Eat first. Think twice. And don’t walk into the first coffee shop you see near the Great Wall. Consider this a friendly warning 😌☕️ PS. Another warning. Souvenirs here are over-priced. If you have bargaining skill, use it!!! I was about to buy a hat which they sell 385yuan. I visited the Mutianyu section, which is known for its beautiful restoration work and slightly fewer crowds than Badaling. The journey up involved a scenic cable car ride, which added to the anticipation before stepping onto the Wall itself. Once you’re up there, it’s hard not to be overwhelmed by the panoramic views. Endless mountain ridges roll out into the distance, with the Wall snaking along their peaks like a living sculpture. The path varies from smooth stone walkways to steep, uneven steps that seem to rise into the clouds. At times, it felt more like a challenging hike than a tourist stroll—but that physical effort made the experience feel even more authentic. Every tower, every step tells a story of ancient dynasties, battles, and the sheer determination it took to build such a massive structure by hand. One of the most striking aspects of the Wall is how it interacts with the natural environment. It blends into the hills and forests, and no matter where you look, the views are cinematic. In summer, the greenery surrounding the Wall is vibrant and lush. In autumn, I’ve heard it’s painted with rich reds and golds. Each season offers something different, and I can only imagine how magical a winter visit would be with snow dusting the ancient stones. There are plenty of rest stops and towers along the way to take breaks, snap photos, or just take in the silence and scale of what surrounds you. It’s both peaceful and powerful.

The Great Wall of China is one of the most iconic and impressive structures ever built by humankind, recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage site and often considered one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. Here's a breakdown of its key aspects: Purpose and History: * Defense: The primary purpose of the Great Wall was military defense. It was built by successive Chinese empires from the 3rd century BC to the 17th century AD to protect their northern borders from invasions and raids by nomadic tribes, such as the Xiongnu and later the Mongols. * Long Construction Period: The wall wasn't built all at once. Construction began as early as the 7th century BC with various states building their own defensive walls. The first emperor of unified China, Qin Shi Huang (around 221-206 BC), ordered the connection and extension of existing walls. Later dynasties, particularly the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644 AD), carried out extensive rebuilding and expansion, creating most of the well-known sections seen today. * Beyond a Wall: It was more than just a wall; it was a complex military defense system including watchtowers, garrisons, signal towers, and fortresses along its length. It also served to protect trade routes, like the Silk Road, and control migration. Dimensions and Construction: * Length: While often cited as "10,000 li" (a traditional Chinese unit of measurement), the official length of all its sections combined is over 21,000 kilometers (13,000 miles). * Materials: Early sections were often built with rammed earth and wood. Later, especially during the Ming Dynasty, more durable materials like bricks, stone, and even granite and marble were used. * Scale: It is one of the largest man-made projects in the world, a testament to the immense human effort, organization, and engineering skills of ancient China. Significance: * Cultural Symbol: The Great Wall has become a powerful and enduring symbol of China, representing the resilience, determination, unity, and ingenuity of the Chinese people. It is deeply embedded in Chinese art, literature, and folklore. * Historical Witness: It bears witness to the rise and fall of empires, the clashes of civilizations, and the continuous struggle for security and control in ancient China. * Tourism: Today, while its military function has ended, it is China's top tourist attraction, drawing millions of visitors each year who are captivated by its historical grandeur and picturesque landscapes. Current Status: * Despite its immense size, parts of the Great Wall are in ruins or have disappeared due to natural erosion and human activities. However, significant sections have been preserved and restored, making them accessible to tourists. The Great Wall of China is not just a physical structure; it is a profound historical and cultural monument that speaks volumes about China's past and its enduring spirit.

Tourist tip: Here at Mutianyu you can go either by an enclosed cable car (up and down) or an open cable car (up and down) or go down with the slide. Your passport is your ticket and then you get a bus to go up to the mountain (5min ride). Once there, you walk up like 10min and arrive at the entrance (and queue) for the open cable car + slide. Continue walking up and you arrive at the entrance of the enclosed one. You'll get your passport scanned one more time and you'll walk to the base of the cable car. Go up by the stairs (or take the lift) and you get (again) your passport scanned and ready to get into the cable car. Once you arrive to the top, you are at the base of tower 14. To the left, you can walk up to tower 23 (very difficult path) or to the right up to tower 1 (quite a few hours walking). At tower 4 is the slide in case you have that ticket. Our tourist guide recommended us to do the open cable car + slide first and then the enclosed one. The queue for the open cable car is long due to only two passengers per car, while you can go up to 10 people in the enclosed one.

1. Length: The Great Wall of China is approximately 13,171 miles (21,196 km) long, making it one of the longest structures ever built. 2. History: The wall was built over several centuries, with the first versions being constructed as early as the 7th century BC. 3. Purpose: The wall was initially built to protect the Chinese Empire from invading armies and to control trade and immigration. 4. Materials: The wall is made from a variety of materials, including stone, brick, rammed earth, and wood. 5. Watchtowers: The wall has over 2,000 watchtowers, which were used for military defense and communication. 6. Construction: It's estimated that over a million workers were involved in building the wall, with many losing their lives during construction. 7. UNESCO World Heritage Site: The Great Wall of China was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. 8. Visible from space: Contrary to popular myth, the Great Wall of China is not visible from space, but it is visible from low Earth orbit. 9. At the foothill, the cable car station is further up than the lift station. So make sure you line up for the correct line. We took cable up to tower 14 and hiked up to 20, via the somewhat steep Hao Han Po. And then walked all the way back to tower 6 to take toboggan down. Unfortunately, the toboggan doesn’t operate in the rain and lift doesn’t operate when there’s lightening. So we had to actually talk down the hill to catch the shuttle, which took about 20 mins. The Mutianyu section of the Great Wall of China is a stunning testament to human ingenuity and determination, and as a Google Local Guide, I can confidently say it’s one of the most captivating historical sites I’ve visited. Mutianyu is renowned for its picturesque surroundings. Nestled among lush forests, this section of the wall offers panoramic views that are nothing short of spectacular. Whether visiting in the vibrant greens of spring and summer, the golden hues of autumn, or the serene snow-covered landscape of winter, Mutianyu provides a breathtaking backdrop to the ancient structure. Compared to other sections like Badaling, Mutianyu is beautifully restored and less crowded, making it ideal for those who want to experience the Great Wall without the hustle and bustle. The stonework and watchtowers are in excellent condition, giving visitors a clear sense of the wall’s original grandeur and purpose. Mutianyu is easily accessible from Beijing, with well-maintained roads and transportation options. The visitor facilities are modern and comprehensive, including a visitor center, restaurants, and shops. The cable car and chairlift provide easy access to the wall for those who might find the climb challenging, while the toboggan ride down adds a fun and memorable twist to the visit. Walking along the wall, you can’t help but be awed by the history that surrounds you. The strategic importance of this section, with its dense watchtowers and steep inclines, is palpable. The information provided on-site, through plaques and guides, enriches the experience, offering insights into the wall’s construction and its role in defending ancient China. Mutianyu is a great choice for families, with activities and facilities that cater to visitors of all ages. The cable car and toboggan make it accessible and enjoyable for children, while the well-marked paths ensure a safe and comfortable visit. For those who prefer a bit of adventure, the hike along the wall is invigorating and rewarding. Mutianyu offers a perfect balance between accessibility, historical authenticity, and natural beauty. Whether you’re a history enthusiast, a photographer, or simply a traveler seeking to connect with one of the world’s most iconic landmarks, Mutianyu delivers an unforgettable experience. Highly recommended for anyone visiting Beijing—it’s an essential part of any trip to China.

We only visited on a layover but would have loved to spend more time here and explore more of the wall hiking a bit further.
The Great Wall of China is the most magical place, filled with stories in every corner, creating an amazing experience.

The best preserved and most spectacular part of the Great Wall of China. You can climb on foot or take a gondola to get you up to the top. You can walk freely on the wall and you can climb up one side and down the other. The view that you enjoy worth every penny . Before arriving at the great wall pass through a bazaar where you can buy all kind of souvenirs. If you visit Beijing you must need to visit the Great Wall, it's amazing

Though has been one of the 7 wonders of the world. Best season to go there are winters. If you go in summer or rain walking is tough and you won't enjoy the walk. There are 2 bus routes ranging 877 and 919. 877 is from badaling and 919 is from mutayin. Both ways are good, you get the bus for both the location from the same place. Please do carry your water bottle with you and some snacks to have. Also there are shopping places near great wall the things are priced not to expensive.
Amazing experience and it’s breathtaking views from the top. It’s a great privilege to visit and see this spectacular place as one of the wonders of the world.

A real remarkable work of architectures and the Landmark of this enchanting city of Beijing. The Great Walls of China is so far one of the great Man-made Wonders of the World that is worth and must to see. Please wear comfortable footwear when strolling along this kilometers winding roads and be sure you are robust and with good physical condition. There are lots to photograph and souvenirs to bring home so take a bigger bag with you :-)
This segment of the Great Wall has been well restored. Nice visitors facilities all around.

If in Beijing MUST MUST MUST visit the visit the Mutianyu section of the Great Wall of China It’s astounding to stand on this wall and look out at the vast distance that it covers, realizing that what you can see is only a tiny portion. To think that it was built with only manpower in almost unbelievable. Everything from the elaborate entrance, the lift ride up to the top and the slide down was amazing, and that wasn’t even the pinnacle of the site. Sitting in the lift and looking around at the scenery really magnified the feat that it was to build the wall. Walking up the stairway and out onto the walkway of the wall is unforgettable and something pictures don’t do justice.

You have to visit this place! Take the ski lift up and the luge down! At the end of the luge, they take a pic and try to sell it to you. But it’s actually a nice keepsake! Lots of tourist souvenirs at the entrance!
Must visit while staying in Beijing. You can hike, go up by cable car or sliding.
You might wait in the queue about 3 hours during public holidays. Slide-way is fun but not much comfortable to ride. You must have passport with you.

I never thought that i will go to the great wall of china as a solo traveller. It was worth it. This was a historical trip. Tells so much about China. And the Muntiayu trail is the best. Few people only. Cable car ride was fun. Met new friends here too who pushed us up til we reach the top. Bring water as you may need it while climbing. Next trail soon!

One of the wonders in the world. Long stretch of wall around china. The steps are pretty steep so be careful. Would recommend to climb when the weather is more chilly cause it is way too tiring to climb during summer.
Beautiful place. Make sure to apply lots of sunscreen and carry ample water. If possible climb up to the highest allowed point and the view there is simply breathtaking.

This is a magnificent piece of history and a fantastic experience. A must do when visiting Beijing. A few things to note that might be helpful in terms of logistics : 1) Parts of it are quite steep or uneven. Wear shoes you are comfortable walking in. 2) We took the tram up and then the slide down. I think the advantage of this is that you don't have to walk back and forth; but rather have a starting and ending point that are different. 3) You can purchase one way tickets - just ask.
